title: Nadella's Nuclear Option: Inside Microsoft's $25 Billion Plan to Swallow OpenAI Whole
excerpt: The Indian-born CEO's testimony in the Musk v. OpenAI trial reveals a high-stakes contingency plan, a $92 billion projected windfall, and an existential fear of becoming 'the next IBM'
body:
When Sam Altman was unceremoniously fired from OpenAI in November 2023, the world saw chaos. Satya Nadella, it turns out, saw an opportunity — and moved to seize it in under 24 hours.

Testifying this month in the blockbuster *Musk v. OpenAI* trial in Oakland, California, Microsoft's Indian-born chief executive revealed that his team had drawn up a $25 billion emergency plan to absorb OpenAI's leadership and talent the moment Altman's ouster became public. The plan was never executed — Altman returned to OpenAI within days — but its very existence illuminates the knife-edge calculations shaping the AI industry's future.

## A bet that could define the decade

Nadella's testimony laid bare how profoundly Microsoft had wagered its future on artificial intelligence. The company's investment in OpenAI, which began with $1 billion in 2019 and swelled to $13 billion by 2023, is now projected to yield returns of $92 billion, according to internal documents presented at trial. That would make it one of the most lucrative corporate bets in the history of technology.

But the Hyderabad-raised executive also admitted to a deeper fear: that Microsoft might become "the next IBM" — a once-dominant technology giant that missed the transition to a new computing paradigm and spent decades in decline. It was this existential anxiety, Nadella suggested, that drove the OpenAI partnership in the first place. Microsoft could not afford to lose the AI race the way IBM lost the cloud.

## 'Amateurish' — and personal

Nadella did not mince words about OpenAI's board, which had fired Altman without consulting Microsoft despite its massive financial stake. He called the move "amateurish" and said he never received a clear explanation for the decision. The episode exposed a fundamental vulnerability: for all its billions, Microsoft had no seat on OpenAI's board and no formal governance control over its most important partner.

The revelation carries particular weight for Indian tech professionals, who have watched Nadella's ascent with pride since he took the helm at Microsoft in 2014. Born in Hyderabad and educated at Manipal and the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, Nadella has become arguably the most powerful Indian-origin executive in global technology — a status this trial has only reinforced.

## Musk's $180 billion gambit

The backdrop to Nadella's testimony is Elon Musk's sprawling lawsuit against OpenAI, which seeks damages of up to $180 billion. Musk, a co-founder of the AI lab, alleges that Altman and his allies betrayed OpenAI's original nonprofit mission by transforming it into a for-profit juggernaut now valued at roughly $850 billion. Microsoft, Musk's lawyers argue, was a willing accomplice — bankrolling the transition in exchange for preferential access to the world's most advanced AI systems.

Nadella pushed back, insisting Microsoft's role was that of a partner, not a puppeteer. He expressed pride in the investment, noting it had helped create "one of the world's largest nonprofits" alongside a commercially viable AI enterprise.

## What the diaspora is watching

For the Indian diaspora, the trial is more than a courtroom drama. It is a referendum on the influence of Indian-origin leaders in Silicon Valley's most consequential decisions. Nadella's willingness to commit $25 billion in a single weekend — and his candour about Microsoft's vulnerabilities — paints a portrait of a CEO who operates with the confidence of someone who has already transformed one of the world's largest companies.

The trial also underscores how far the AI gold rush has come from its academic origins. OpenAI began as a nonprofit laboratory dedicated to ensuring artificial intelligence benefits humanity. Today it is the centrepiece of a legal battle involving hundreds of billions of dollars, the egos of the world's richest men, and the future of a technology that could reshape every industry on earth.

The jury in Oakland is expected to deliver its verdict within weeks. Whatever it decides, Nadella's testimony has already delivered a clear message: in the AI era, the line between partnership and absorption is thinner than anyone imagined — and it was an Indian-born engineer who nearly erased it altogether.
